content: When an object moves farther from a converging lens, I know the real image approaches the focal region. How does that happen if the focal point itself is fixed by the lens?

The focal point stays fixed; it is the image distance that changes. Rays from a very distant object arrive nearly parallel and converge close to the focal plane. For a nearer object, the rays reach the lens with more divergence, so the lens needs a longer distance after refraction to bring them together.
How does the lens account for that extra divergence? In a ray diagram, the principal rays look like special paths, almost as though only those rays are being focused.

The principal rays are just convenient representatives. Every ray from one object point is refracted according to the local surface angle and refractive index. If the lens is ideal, all those outgoing rays meet at the same image point. The three standard rays let you locate that point without tracing the full bundle.
When the object is at twice the focal length, the image is the same size and inverted. Why does moving inward make the magnification grow while the image keeps flipping direction?

For an object outside the focal length, the rays truly cross, so the real image remains inverted. As the object approaches the focal point, the outgoing bundle converges more weakly and meets farther away. That larger image distance relative to object distance gives a larger magnitude of magnification; the negative sign records the inversion.
How should I picture the transition right at the focal distance? Does the image briefly sit at infinity, or is infinity only shorthand for rays that no longer intersect?

It is both a mathematical limit and a useful physical description. At exactly one focal length, an ideal thin lens sends rays from each object point out parallel, so no finite screen can catch a focused image. Saying the image is at infinity describes that collimated bundle rather than a literal surface located infinitely far away.
A lens has two refracting surfaces, but diagrams often replace both with one bend at the center line. How do the two surface refractions combine into a single focusing action?

At the first surface, a ray changes direction as it enters the glass; at the second, it changes again as it returns to air. The curvatures make those changes depend on ray height. In the thin-lens approximation, the separation between surfaces is neglected, so the two direction changes can be represented by one equivalent bend.
When a ray enters near the upper edge, the surface normal tilts more than near the axis. Is that larger incident angle what gives the edge a stronger focal power?

Broadly, yes: the changing normal across a curved surface gives different rays different deflections, steering them toward a common point. But edge rays do not simply receive a perfectly proportional increase. For a spherical lens they often cross at a slightly different location, producing spherical aberration beyond the paraxial approximation.
How does the second surface help instead of undoing the first bend? Since the ray goes from glass back into air, I would expect the refraction direction to reverse.

The ray does bend away from the normal when leaving glass, but the second surface's normal points in a different direction. For a biconvex lens, that geometry usually bends the ray farther toward the optical axis. Reversing the index step does not reverse the whole path unless the interface orientation is also reversed appropriately.
If the lens were immersed in water, when would those two bends become too weak to form a nearby image? The glass still has curvature, but its relative index is smaller.

It still forms an image as long as the glass and water have different refractive indices, but the focal length becomes longer. Focusing vanishes in the limit where their indices match, because neither interface changes the ray direction. If the surrounding medium had a higher index than the lens, the lens's converging or diverging role could even reverse.
How thick can the glass become before the single central bend stops being a reliable model? Is thickness judged against focal length, surface radius, or the object distance?

There is no universal cutoff, but thickness matters when the distance traveled inside the lens is no longer negligible for the required accuracy. Comparing center thickness with curvature radii and focal length is usually more relevant than comparing it with object distance. Then you use two refracting surfaces or principal planes instead of one lens plane.
With a magnifying glass, the object is inside the focal length and the image is called virtual. How does an image have a definite position if no rays actually meet there?

After the lens, rays from each object point diverge, but they do so as if they originated from a particular point behind the object. Extending those rays backward locates that point. Your eye receives the diverging bundle and interprets it using the same directional cues it normally uses for light from a real object.
When I move the magnifier closer to the object, the enlarged view sometimes seems smaller. Is the virtual image sliding toward the lens even though the angular magnification can still change?

Yes. Deep inside the focal length, bringing the object closer to the lens moves the virtual image closer and reduces its linear magnification. What your eye perceives also depends on angular size and viewing distance. A smaller virtual image can still subtend a useful angle if its apparent position and the lens position are close enough.
How does my eye focus on that backward extension? It sounds as though the lens creates an imaginary object that the eye then projects onto the retina as a real image.

That is nearly the right chain. The magnifier produces a diverging bundle with the same vergence as light from the virtual image location. The eye accommodates for that vergence and its own lens forms a real image on the retina. Nothing is projected backward; the virtual location summarizes the directions of the rays entering the eye.
When could a second lens turn that virtual image into something visible on a screen? Would the virtual image act as the second lens's object, or does its sign change again?

A second converging lens can redirect the bundle so it converges onto a screen. For that lens, the incoming rays determine whether its object is real or virtual: if they are diverging from a point on the incoming side, that point is a real object for it. The signs depend on the convention, but the ray geometry is unambiguous.
How is that different from placing a screen where the virtual image appears? The location seems geometrically specified, so I would expect some concentrated light there.

The apparent location lies on the backward extensions, not on the actual outgoing paths. A screen there intercepts light before or on the wrong side of the lens, where rays from each object point have not converged. A real image requires actual rays from each point to meet at corresponding points on the screen.
When the object reaches the focal point, does the virtual image switch sides discontinuously? The lens equation changes sign, but the ray bundle seems as though it should evolve smoothly.

The bundle evolves smoothly. Approaching the focal point from inside sends the virtual image farther away; at the focal point the rays are parallel; just outside, they converge to a very distant real image on the opposite side. The algebraic image distance passes through infinity, so the side change is not a finite jump.
For two lenses made from the same glass, how does stronger curvature shorten the focal length? I understand that steeper surfaces refract more, but not when that becomes a linear effect.

Stronger curvature means smaller radii, so the surface normals rotate more rapidly with distance from the axis. In the paraxial limit, the lensmaker relation makes optical power proportional to combinations of inverse radii, multiplied by the refractive-index contrast. The relationship is linear in power, not generally in focal length, because power equals one over focal length.
When both radii are halved for a symmetric biconvex lens, should I expect twice the focusing strength and therefore half the focal distance, assuming the lens stays thin?

Under the thin-lens and paraxial assumptions, yes. Halving both signed radii doubles each inverse-radius term, so the optical power doubles and the focal length halves. In a real lens, changing curvature while holding thickness negligible may be impossible, and stronger curvature also increases aberrations that the simple relation does not describe.
How does a plano-convex lens compare if its curved side has the same radius as either side of that symmetric lens? Does the flat face contribute zero refraction?

The flat face has zero surface power in the lensmaker formula because its radius is infinite, but a ray can still change direction there if it arrives obliquely. For near-axis collimated light, a plano-convex lens with one matching curved radius has about half the power of a symmetric biconvex lens whose two surfaces contribute equally.
When does the orientation of that plano-convex lens matter? Its focal length should be the same either way, yet one direction is said to focus more cleanly.

Its paraxial focal length is essentially unchanged when flipped, but spherical aberration changes. For collimated light focused to a point, placing the curved surface toward the collimated beam usually distributes refraction more favorably between the surfaces. The best orientation depends on the conjugate distances, not on a change in first-order optical power.
The thin-lens equation often uses positive and negative image distances. How does the sign encode the physical image without making the equation depend on which direction I draw the page?

A sign convention ties signs to light propagation and to whether rays actually converge or only appear to diverge from a point. Different conventions exist, so the page orientation is irrelevant as long as definitions remain consistent. A common real-is-positive convention assigns positive distance to real objects and images and negative distance to virtual ones.
When magnification is negative, I read that as an inverted image. Is that negative value a direction of magnification, or only bookkeeping inherited from the height coordinates?

It is bookkeeping with physical meaning. Transverse magnification is the signed ratio of image height to object height. A negative ratio says corresponding points lie on opposite sides of the optical axis, so the image is inverted in that transverse direction. The magnitude tells the size ratio; magnification itself is not a spatial direction.
How does the formula distinguish an upright virtual image from an upright real one? Positive magnification seems to describe both possibilities if another optical element flips the object first.

Magnification alone cannot classify the image as real or virtual. Its sign only compares orientation with the chosen object. You also need the image-distance sign or the actual ray vergence. In a multi-element system, an intermediate image may serve as an object for the next element, so orientation and reality must be tracked separately.
When I switch to the Cartesian convention, why do some familiar formulas acquire extra minus signs? The rays have not changed, so I assume the focal power is being relabeled.

Exactly: the optics is unchanged, while coordinate definitions change. In a Cartesian convention, distances measured along one axis direction are positive and those measured opposite are negative. The algebra must reflect those choices, including signed focal lengths and radii. Rather than transferring signs between formulas, derive or record one internally consistent set.
How can I check a result without relying on memorized signs? Is drawing whether the outgoing rays converge or diverge enough to recover the image type and orientation?

A quick ray sketch is an excellent check. Determine whether outgoing rays converge to a real image or require backward extensions for a virtual one, then compare an off-axis object's image point with the axis to determine orientation. The equation should agree. A limiting case, such as an object very far away, provides another reliable check.
Closing a camera aperture makes the image dimmer, which is clear, but how does it also make more distances look focused when the lens still has one image plane?

Only one object plane is exactly conjugate to the sensor plane. Points away from that plane form small blur disks instead of points. A smaller aperture narrows each cone of rays, so those disks become smaller at the fixed sensor. More object distances then fall below your chosen sharpness threshold, creating greater depth of field.
When the aperture becomes very small, could every object distance become exactly sharp because the ray cones approach single lines? Or is that only increasing the acceptable focus zone?

It only increases the range that appears acceptably sharp. Geometric blur shrinks, but exact image distances remain different for different object distances. Moreover, a very small aperture introduces diffraction: each point spreads into an Airy pattern. Eventually diffraction softening grows enough that stopping down further reduces overall detail rather than improving it.
How does the circle of confusion relate to the lens equation? I tend to think of it as the focal spot getting wider, although the ideal convergence point is elsewhere.

The lens equation gives the axial location where an ideal point's cone would converge. If the sensor sits before or after that location, it cuts the cone at a finite cross-section: the circle of confusion. Its diameter follows from similar triangles and depends on aperture diameter and the separation between the sensor and ideal image plane.
When does changing aperture move the actual focus? In the ideal model it should not, but real photographs sometimes show a small focus shift after stopping down.

An ideal thin lens has no aperture-dependent focal position. Real lenses with spherical aberration focus marginal and paraxial rays at slightly different distances. A wide aperture includes both; stopping down removes more marginal rays, shifting the location of best compromise focus. Lens design and focus breathing can complicate the observed shift further.
How is the depth of field split in front of and behind the focused distance? People say one third and two thirds, but that sounds like a fixed focusing ratio.

The one-third/two-thirds rule is only a rough special case. The distribution depends on focal length, aperture, focus distance, and the allowed circle of confusion. At close distances it is closer to symmetric around the focused plane; near the hyperfocal distance, the far region can extend to infinity while the near region remains finite.
When focusing at the hyperfocal distance, is infinity literally on the same image plane, or merely blurred by exactly the maximum circle that was declared acceptable?

Infinity is not exactly focused unless the lens is set to infinity. At the hyperfocal setting, the sensor lies slightly away from infinity's ideal focal plane, so distant points form circles of confusion at the selected acceptable limit. The usefulness of the setting therefore depends on viewing size, resolution, eyesight, and the chosen sharpness criterion.
White light passing through a simple lens forms colored fringes near focus. How does dispersion turn one focal point into several if every color crosses the same curved surfaces?

The surfaces are the same, but the glass's refractive index varies with wavelength. Shorter wavelengths usually experience a larger index and therefore greater optical power, reaching focus closer to a positive lens. Each spectral band has its own focal distance, producing longitudinal color blur and, away from the center, differently scaled images.
When the sensor is placed between the red and blue focal planes, why can a green edge appear beside a magenta one? I expected separate colored copies instead of paired borders.

A defocused wavelength spreads light across an edge rather than making a clearly separated copy. At a chosen sensor plane, some wavelengths may be tighter while others spill to opposite sides of high-contrast transitions. Their additive combinations can produce green on one side and magenta on the other, depending on focus position and lens correction.
How does an achromatic doublet bring two colors together? Is the diverging element adding negative dispersion while preserving most of the first lens's positive convergence?

That is the basic strategy. A positive low-dispersion crown element is paired with a negative higher-dispersion flint element. Their powers are chosen so the combined system remains converging while their wavelength-dependent power changes cancel at two selected wavelengths. Other wavelengths still have residual secondary spectrum, so the correction is not perfect.
When would lateral chromatic aberration remain even if axial colors share a focus? Does it come from wavelength-dependent magnification rather than a different focal surface?

Yes. Lateral chromatic aberration is mainly a wavelength-dependent image scale, so red, green, and blue versions of an off-axis point land at different transverse positions. It grows toward the field edges and is not removed simply by choosing another sensor plane. Correcting it requires controlling chromatic power across the whole optical system.
A spherical lens does not bring all parallel rays to exactly one point. How do marginal rays end up focusing sooner when the surface is supposed to have one constant curvature?

Constant curvature means the surface belongs to a sphere, not that every ray experiences an equivalent geometry. Farther from the axis, surface normals are tilted more strongly, and Snell's law produces deviations that depart from the paraxial linear relation. For a typical positive spherical lens, marginal rays therefore cross the axis closer to the lens.
When texts restrict rays to the paraxial region in practice, are they making Snell's law approximate, or only replacing the trigonometric angles with small-angle versions?

Snell's law itself remains exact. The paraxial treatment approximates sines and tangents by their angles and keeps only first-order terms in ray height and angle. Under those assumptions, refraction becomes linear and all rays from an object point share one Gaussian image point. Higher-order terms describe aberrations such as spherical aberration.
How does an aspheric surface correct the marginal focus? I picture its outer zones being flatter, but I am unsure whether that is always the required shape.

An asphere changes the normal directions zone by zone so marginal rays receive the deflection needed to meet the paraxial focus. For a given positive-lens task, that often means departing from the spherical profile in a way that reduces excessive edge bending, but the exact sag can be steeper or flatter depending on indices and conjugates.
When I stop the lens down, does spherical aberration disappear or just become hidden because the aperture rejects the rays with the wrong focal length?

It is mostly suppressed rather than corrected. The physical surface still gives different zones different focal behavior, but a smaller stop blocks the marginal zones that contribute the largest error. The remaining rays form a tighter spot, at the cost of light and eventually diffraction. Residual aberration can persist even within the reduced aperture.
How is the best focus chosen when the rays cross over a range of distances? Is it the smallest geometric disk, or does diffraction change where that focus plane belongs?

Geometrically, one common choice is the plane of least confusion, where the ray bundle has its smallest cross-section. For actual imaging, best focus depends on the metric: peak intensity, contrast at a chosen spatial frequency, or total wavefront error can select slightly different planes. Diffraction combines with aberration, so wave-optical optimization is more meaningful.
When two thin lenses are separated, how does the first image become the object for the second? I can combine their powers only when they are touching, so the gap seems optically active.

Trace the first lens independently to find where its rays would converge. At the second lens, those incoming rays may still be converging, already diverging, or exactly focused there. Their vergence defines the second lens's object distance. The air gap changes that vergence through propagation, which is why separated powers cannot simply be added.
How can the second lens have a virtual object if the first lens is forming a real image? Is that when the second lens intercepts the rays before their crossing point?

Exactly. If the second lens sits before the first lens's intended real image, its incoming rays are converging toward a point on its outgoing side. That point is a virtual object for the second lens. The label refers to where the rays are headed before refraction, not to whether the upstream lens was capable of forming a real image.
When does the pair become afocal? I know the separation is related to the two focal lengths, but I sometimes treat that as the lenses sharing one focus.

An afocal pair converts a parallel input bundle into a parallel output bundle. For two positive thin lenses, that occurs when their separation equals the sum of their focal lengths: the rear focal point of the first coincides with the front focal point of the second. They share a focal plane, not a single focal point belonging to both.
How does an afocal telescope enlarge an image if the final rays are still parallel? There is no final real image until the eye or another lens receives them.

It enlarges angularly rather than producing a larger final plane image by itself. The objective turns each distant field angle into a position at the shared focal plane. The eyepiece converts that position back into a different outgoing angle. Your eye then focuses the parallel bundle onto the retina, where the larger angle produces a larger retinal image.
When one lens in the pair is negative, why is the afocal spacing a difference rather than a sum? Does the virtual focal point count as a negative physical gap?

The focal lengths are signed, so the same algebraic condition can be written as a signed sum. A negative lens has a virtual focal point on the side from which collimated light arrives. The physical spacing stays positive; the negative focal length reduces the required distance because the relevant focal locations lie differently along the axis.
How would moving the lenses slightly away from the afocal spacing show up in the output? Would distant objects gain a finite image distance, or mainly look out of focus to the eye?

The output acquires nonzero vergence, so a collimated input no longer leaves collimated. It then has a finite real or virtual focus depending on the direction of the spacing error. An accommodating eye may compensate for a modest error, making the view seem focused but less comfortable; a camera fixed at infinity would record defocus.
The eye keeps the retinal distance nearly fixed, yet it focuses from distant objects to nearby ones. How does accommodation alter the lens equation without moving the image screen?

Accommodation changes the eye's optical power. The ciliary system allows the crystalline lens to become more curved for near objects, shortening its effective focal length so the image still lands on the retina. For distant objects, the lens is flatter and weaker. The retina stays fixed while the object distance and focal power trade off.
When the crystalline lens becomes rounder, is most of the added refraction at its front surface? I assume the cornea remains the stronger fixed focusing element.

The cornea supplies most of the eye's total static power because of the large air-to-cornea index change. Accommodation comes from shape changes in the crystalline lens, involving both surfaces and its internal gradient of refractive index. The front-surface curvature changes noticeably, but assigning all added power to one interface is too simple.
How does farsightedness interfere with that process? Is the relaxed focal point behind the retina, requiring accommodation to pull the image forward even for distant light?

In hyperopia, the eye is too weak or too short for its relaxed power, so parallel rays would focus behind the retina. A person with sufficient accommodation can add power and bring distant images forward onto the retina, then add still more for near objects. This extra demand can become difficult as accommodative range decreases.
When a positive corrective lens is added, how does it avoid forming an image before light reaches the eye? Is it creating a virtual object at the eye's far point?

For ordinary viewing, the positive spectacle or contact lens gives incoming rays some convergence but does not bring them to a focus before the eye. The eye receives a bundle equivalent to one from an object within its focusing range. Describing the correction through the eye's far point is especially useful for refractive errors and lens prescriptions.
A projector produces a real enlarged image on a screen. How does moving the projector lens a few millimeters bring a distant screen into focus when the object slide barely changes position?

The slide or imaging panel sits only slightly beyond the lens's focal plane. In that region, a small change in object-to-lens spacing causes a much larger change in image distance. Moving the lens changes both conjugate distances, allowing the real image plane to coincide with the screen while the projector body remains essentially fixed.
When the screen is moved farther away, does the projected image necessarily become larger? I think the magnification grows, but the lens may also need to move toward the slide.

For a fixed lens and slide, increasing the required image distance generally increases the magnitude of magnification. Refocusing requires the slide-to-lens distance to move closer to one focal length, so the lens usually shifts relative to the slide. Practical projectors may move internal groups, but the conjugate relation still produces a larger image at longer throw.
How does the screen receive every image point without also showing the crossing rays from neighboring points as a haze? Those rays occupy the same space near the lens.

Ray bundles from many object points overlap in space, but direction carries their information. The lens redirects each bundle so rays from one object point reconverge at one corresponding screen point. At the correct plane, neighboring bundles have different convergence centers. Scattering by the screen then sends light from each formed point toward many viewers.
When someone blocks half the projector lens, why does the whole image remain instead of losing half its field? I would expect each lens region to own a section of the picture.

Each small region of the lens receives rays from nearly every point on the slide, so it contributes to the whole image rather than one field section. Blocking half removes part of every point's ray bundle. The complete image remains but becomes dimmer, and its diffraction and aberration pattern may change slightly.
How does keystone distortion fit into lens image formation? The top and bottom are focused by the same lens, yet a tilted screen gives them different magnifications.

A tilted screen intersects the projected ray geometry at different distances across its height. The farther portion samples the expanding image bundle later and therefore at a larger scale than the nearer portion. It may also lie outside the best-focus plane. Keystone correction prewarps the source or shifts optical geometry; it is not ordinary uniform lens magnification.
In a camera, how does moving the sensor relative to the lens select one object distance? Light from all distances enters together, so I am unclear how one plane gets priority.

The lens creates a different ideal image distance for each object distance. Placing the sensor at one of those image planes makes rays from that object plane converge sharply on its surface. Rays from nearer or farther objects cross before or after the sensor, so the sensor intercepts them as blur disks rather than points.
When autofocus moves a lens group instead of the sensor, is it changing focal length or merely shifting the back focal plane? The two effects seem mixed in a compound lens.

In an ideal unit-focus lens, moving the whole lens changes its distance to the sensor without changing focal length. Internal-focus designs move selected groups, which changes the system's principal planes and often its effective focal length slightly. Thus the image plane is repositioned, but magnification and field of view can also change, producing focus breathing.
How does the sensor distinguish a slightly defocused point from a physically larger object detail? Both could cover several pixels with a similar intensity patch.

A single isolated patch may be ambiguous. Focus systems use broader evidence: phase-detection compares rays from different pupil regions to estimate the direction and amount of defocus, while contrast detection searches for the lens position that maximizes fine spatial contrast. Scene structure, multiple edges, and sometimes learned priors help separate blur from object size.
When phase detection says focus is in front or behind, how do two pupil samples encode that sign? Are they effectively viewing two shifted versions of the image?

Yes. Opposite parts of the pupil provide two sub-aperture views. If the sensor plane is displaced from the true image plane, the two views show corresponding features shifted relative to each other. The direction of that disparity indicates front or back focus, and its magnitude estimates how far the focusing group should move.
How does pixel size enter the acceptable focus calculation? A circle of confusion smaller than one pixel sounds invisible, but sampling and color filters may complicate that cutoff.

Pixel pitch sets one relevant scale, but not a hard visibility boundary. The optical point-spread function, antialiasing filter, color-filter mosaic, demosaicing, sharpening, and display enlargement all affect recorded detail. A blur diameter below one pixel can still reduce contrast near the sampling limit, while a larger blur may be unnoticed in a small output.
When the lens is focused beyond infinity, what image geometry is actually occurring? Infinity has no farther object distance, so the phrase seems to describe a sensor offset rather than a subject.

Correct. Focusing beyond infinity means the optical system is set so parallel incoming rays would come to focus on the wrong side of the sensor plane, usually because the lens is positioned slightly too close to the sensor. Lenses allow this extra travel to accommodate thermal expansion, wavelength shifts, manufacturing tolerances, and autofocus control margin.
An off-axis object point still forms an image point, but its rays are asymmetric through the lens. How does that asymmetry create coma instead of merely shifting the image sideways?

For an ideal paraxial lens, the asymmetry only maps field angle to image height. In a real system, different annular zones and azimuths of the pupil give slightly different transverse magnifications for an off-axis point. Their images do not coincide, producing a bright core with a one-sided tail resembling a comet.
When the aperture is narrowed, why does the comet tail shrink? Is coma another edge-ray focus error, or does the stop change which magnifications participate?

Both descriptions point to the same pupil dependence. Coma is a field-dependent aberration whose transverse error grows strongly with aperture. Stopping down removes outer pupil zones, reducing the spread of their differing image locations and therefore shortening the tail. The underlying lens remains comatic, and diffraction eventually limits further improvement.
How does field curvature differ from coma? I sometimes describe curved-field blur as the edge rays focusing closer, but that sounds similar to spherical aberration.

Field curvature concerns the best-focus surface across image height: even well-formed off-axis points may lie on a curved surface rather than a flat sensor. Spherical aberration concerns pupil zones for one object point, including on-axis points. Coma is an asymmetric pupil-dependent spread that grows off-axis. Calling all three edge-ray errors hides which edge is meant.
When a curved sensor matches that field in practice, would off-axis points become fully sharp, or would astigmatism still give separate tangential and sagittal focus shells?

A suitably curved sensor can remove defocus caused by the average field curvature, but it cannot automatically eliminate other aberrations. With astigmatism, tangential and sagittal ray fans focus on different surfaces, so no single sensor shape coincides perfectly with both. Optical correction is still needed to bring those surfaces together and control coma.
For a thick lens, focal length is measured from a principal plane rather than from the glass surface. How does an imaginary plane acquire a real role in forming the image?

A principal plane is an equivalent reference plane, not a physical refracting surface. The two real surfaces and the propagation between them transform paraxial rays in a way that can be represented by refraction at paired planes. Measuring object and image distances from those planes lets the familiar thin-lens equations reproduce the system's first-order behavior.
When can a principal plane lie outside the lens itself? That seems to place the effective bend in air, where the refractive index is not changing.

It can lie outside whenever the combined ray transformation requires that equivalent geometry. Strongly curved thick elements and separated compound groups commonly produce this. No bend actually occurs at the external plane; it is where extrapolated incoming and outgoing paraxial rays give the convenient unity-magnification mapping used to define conjugate distances.
How does the back focal length then differ from the effective focal length? I have treated both as the sensor distance for an object at infinity.

Effective focal length is measured from the rear principal plane to the rear focal point. Back focal length is measured from the last physical optical surface to that same focal point. They are equal only if the rear principal plane coincides with the last surface. Mechanical camera clearance depends on back focal length, while image scale depends on effective focal length.
When a telephoto design is physically shorter than its stated focal length, is that mainly because its rear principal plane has shifted forward beyond the lens barrel?

The key is that positive and negative groups shift the principal planes so the effective focal length exceeds the physical distance from the optics to the image. Depending on the design and reference direction, saying simply that one plane shifts forward can be ambiguous. The group combination, rather than a long empty propagation distance, supplies the required angular magnification.
How are principal planes found in practice? Could I trace one parallel ray and one central ray, or does a thick lens require a full matrix calculation?

In first-order optics, either method works. You can trace suitable paraxial rays through every surface, extend the input and output segments, and infer focal points and principal planes from their intersections. An ABCD ray-transfer matrix packages the same calculation more systematically and is especially convenient for many surfaces, spacings, and different surrounding media.
If every point on an object sends light in many directions, how does a lens preserve which rays belong to which point after all the bundles overlap inside the glass?

The bundles can overlap spatially without losing their directions or phases. Refraction acts locally on each ray according to its incident direction and position. For each object point, the lens transforms its particular bundle toward a corresponding image point. Light does not need labels; the optical mapping is carried by position, direction, wavelength, and phase.
When rays from two object points cross before reaching the lens, have their image coordinates already mixed? A screen at that crossing would record both contributions at one place.

A bare screen at the crossing sums whatever light reaches each location, so it may not resolve the source points there. But crossing rays continue with their own directions. The lens uses both arrival position and direction to redirect them. In phase-space terms, sharing one position does not mean sharing the same optical state or destination.
How does blocking half a lens leave every object point represented? I understand that each point illuminates the whole aperture, but does the remaining half change the viewing angle of the image?

For an ordinary image plane, the remaining aperture still directs rays from every object point to its corresponding image point, so the field of view is largely unchanged. What changes is the pupil sampling: brightness falls, diffraction broadens, and aberrations may become asymmetric. Perspective is set mainly by the entrance-pupil position, which may shift slightly in a complex system.
When would covering part of the lens actually remove part of the image? Would that require the obstruction to be near an intermediate image plane instead of an aperture plane?

Yes. Near an aperture or pupil plane, position corresponds mainly to ray angle, so blocking a region affects light from nearly the whole field. Near an image plane, position corresponds mainly to object position, so an obstruction can remove a localized part of the image. Between those planes, it can cause a mixture of vignetting and field clipping.
How does this relate to a pinhole camera, where there is no refracting lens? The aperture seems to choose one ray per object point and thereby create the image mapping.

A pinhole forms the mapping by geometric selection rather than refraction. Ideally, only a narrow range of directions from each object point reaches each screen point, creating an inverted projection. A lens accepts a much wider bundle and redirects it to the same image point, greatly increasing brightness. A finite pinhole trades geometric blur against diffraction.
When the lens is badly defocused, does it approach the pinhole mapping if I close the aperture enough, or are focus and projection still fundamentally different operations?

Closing the aperture reduces the angular range, so defocus blur shrinks and the system behaves more like a pinhole camera geometrically. The lens still refracts the admitted rays, however, and its focused plane remains privileged. In the limit of a very small stop, diffraction dominates, so the resemblance never becomes a perfect sharp projection.
